title: Efficacy of the pentavalent rotavirus vaccine, RotaTeq®, in Finnish infants up to 3 years of age: the Finnish Extension Study.
ehr_evidence: in FES, episodes of AGE requiring hospitalisation or an ED visit were collected at prespecified 12-week intervals by automated short message service contacts, sent via mobile phones, or by direct telephone calls for those without access to text messaging, rather than at 6-week intervals as in REST.
summary: In this randomised placebo-controlled trial extension study (FES), Finnish infants who received the pentavalent rotavirus vaccine (RV5/RotaTeq) or placebo were followed for rotavirus gastroenteritis (RVGE) hospitalisations and emergency department visits up to 3.1 years, showing sustained high vaccine efficacy.
key_findings: Overall RV5 reduced combined RVGE hospitalisations and ED visits by 93.8% (95% CI: 90.8–95.9%) for up to 3.1 years following the last vaccine dose.

Vaccine efficacy against combined hospitalisations and ED visits was 93.9% (95% CI: 89.1–96.9%) at 4–11 months, 94.4% (95% CI: 90.2–97.0%) at 12–23 months, and 85.9% (95% CI: 51.6–97.2%) at 24–35 months.
RV5 reduced hospitalisations and ED visits due to any acute gastroenteritis (rotavirus or not) by 62.4% (95% CI: 57.6–66.6%) over the entire follow-up period.
In the per-protocol population, RV5 reduced the rate of RVGE hospitalisations and ED visits by 94.5% (95% CI: 91.2–96.9).
Against G1 rotaviruses, RV5 reduced combined hospitalisations and ED visits by 95.3% (95% CI: 92.5–97.2%).
Efficacy against G4 rotaviruses was 66.8% (95% CI: <0–94.2%) but not significant, and too few G2 encounters existed to demonstrate efficacy.
There were no cases of intussusception during the FES period.
captured_features: Rotavirus serotype/genotype (G1, G2, G3, G4, G9)
Age of child at health care encounter
study_design: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial with a Finnish Extension Study (FES) follow-up cohort
data_source_type: other (prospective clinical trial follow-up via phone/SMS contacts and case report forms)
population: Finnish infants enrolled in REST at 6–12 weeks of age, followed through FES up to 3.1 years post-vaccination (≈3.5 years of age); 21,151 in the large-scale safety study with 20,732 transitioning into FES
limitations: The clinical-efficacy cohort did not transition into FES, so severity of rotavirus disease was not determined.
Wide confidence intervals in the third year of life due to very few RVGE cases, preventing definitive conclusions beyond 24 months.
Rolling enrollment led to differing durations of follow-up among subjects.
G2 rotavirus was rare at the time, leaving too few encounters to demonstrate efficacy.
